Bowmen
bō´měn
n. pl. (archers; the arm of an army whose noise empties a city)
From bow + men. The Hebrew is romeh qesheth, casters of the bow — archers. The bow is the ranged weapon of the ancient world, and Scripture regularly makes it the emblem of a strength that can fail at a distance from the enemy.

Biblical Definition

Jeremiah describes an invasion by its sound: “The whole city shall flee for the noise of the horsemen and bowmen; they shall go into thickets, and climb up upon the rocks: every city shall be forsaken, and not a man dwell therein” (Jeremiah 4:29). The archers do not need to arrive; their noise empties the towns. The same prophet later turns the bow against the great empire itself: “Put yourselves in array against Babylon round about: all ye that bend the bow, shoot at her, spare no arrows: for she hath sinned against the LORD” (Jeremiah 50:14). Chronicles records the skill at its height in Israel, and it was formidable: “They were armed with bows, and could use both the right hand and the left in hurling stones and shooting arrows out of a bow, even of Saul's brethren of Benjamin” (1 Chronicles 12:2) — ambidextrous Benjamite archers, the elite of David's outlaw band. And the Psalmist records the same arm in failure, with the reason given in the next verse: “The children of Ephraim, being armed, and carrying bows, turned back in the day of battle” (Psalm 78:9). They were armed and they turned back, because they kept not the covenant of God and refused to walk in His law. Equipment was never the variable.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a bowman as a man who uses a bow; an archer.

expand to see more

BOWMAN, n. A man who uses a bow; an archer.

ARCHER, n. [Fr. archer, from L. arcus, a bow.] One who uses a bow; a bowman; one who shoots with a bow.

BOW, n. An instrument of war and hunting, made of wood or other elastic matter, with a string fastened to each end.

QUIVER, n. A case or sheath for arrows.

ARRAY, v.t. To place or dispose in order, as troops for battle.

Key Scripture

Jeremiah 4:29 — "The whole city shall flee for the noise of the horsemen and bowmen; they shall go into thickets, and climb up upon the rocks: every city shall be forsaken, and not a man dwell therein."

Jeremiah 50:14 — "Put yourselves in array against Babylon round about: all ye that bend the bow, shoot at her, spare no arrows: for she hath sinned against the LORD."

1 Chronicles 12:2 — "They were armed with bows, and could use both the right hand and the left in hurling stones and shooting arrows out of a bow, even of Saul's brethren of Benjamin."

Psalm 78:9 — "The children of Ephraim, being armed, and carrying bows, turned back in the day of battle."

Modern Corruption

Failure in the day of battle is diagnosed as a want of preparation, when the Psalmist attributes it to a covenant not kept by men who were fully armed.

expand to see more

Psalm 78:9 is a verse the competent find uncomfortable. Ephraim was armed. Ephraim carried bows. Ephraim turned back. The psalm supplies the reason across the next three verses — they kept not the covenant of God, refused to walk in his law, and forgot his works — and none of the three is a training deficiency. A church can be doctrinally equipped, historically informed, and institutionally sound, and turn back, and the deficiency will not be found in the armoury.

Jeremiah 50:14 supplies the other half of the doctrine and keeps it from fatalism. Babylon is to be shot at, with no arrows spared, because she hath sinned against the LORD — God's judgment on an empire arrives through men who bend actual bows. Providence does not cancel means; it employs them. The Benjamite archers of 1 Chronicles 12:2 are described with real admiration for real skill. Scripture is not embarrassed by competence. It simply refuses to make competence the thing that decides the day.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew romeh qesheth (H7411 + H7198), bow-casters, archers; chets (H2671), an arrow; darak (H1869), to tread, to bend a bow.

expand to see more

Hebrew qesheth (H7198) — a bow; the ranged arm of every ancient army.

Hebrew romeh (H7411) — caster, shooter; Jeremiah 4:29, rendered bowmen.

Hebrew darak qesheth (H1869) — to tread the bow, i.e. to bend it by foot; Jeremiah 50:14.

Hebrew chets (H2671) — an arrow; Psalm 127:4, children as arrows in the hand.

Hebrew nashaq (H5401) — to be armed, equipped; Psalm 78:9, Ephraim armed and turning back.

Usage

"“The noise of the horsemen and bowmen” — the sound alone empties the towns."

"“Being armed, and carrying bows, turned back” — equipment was not the variable."

"“Spare no arrows: for she hath sinned against the LORD” — judgment through means."
